newsitem.title: UK: Gas reinjection plant reopens N.Sea J-Block dispute.
newsitem.headline: Gas reinjection plant reopens N.Sea J-Block dispute.

text.p: The imminent launch of a new gas reinjection module, on schedule for December 20 and now nearing completion at a construction yard in northeast England, is the latest twist in the dispute between the owners of the North Sea's J-Block and Enron Corp, the project's gas buyer.

J-Block operator Phillips Petroleum Co UK Ltd took journalists over the new gas module on Tuesday, less than 15 months after the decision was taken to build the unit and a mere eight months since construction started at AMEC's Wallsend yard on Tyneside.

The dispute between Enron, the single buyer to which all gas reserves are dedicated, and the J-Block owners involves deliveries of gas from the block's Judy and Joanne fields. Enron said in September 1995 that its estimated future total daily nomination for delivery of J-Block gas through September 1997 was zero.

Enron bought the gas under long-term "take or pay" agreements, according to Phillips, and under the agreements, it is required to pay for gas at a predetermined rate even if it elects not to take actual delivery.
By electing to take no gas at all, Enron left Phillips with a problem over how to extract oil, since this could not then be done without also producing gas -- which Enron said it did not want.
Phillips said at the time in a statement: "As both gas and liquids are produced in association with each other, crude oil and condensate volumes will fluctuate with gas production.
"Accordingly, the exact timing of production from J-Block remains uncertain and depends largely on the gas purchaser's elections and alternative production plans being evaluated by J-Block owners."

The alternative production plan with which they came up was to build a reinjection module, so allowing Phillips to produce liquids but send the gas back into the reservoir, where it will remain until Enron elects to bring it ashore.

The 700-tonne unit, with capacity for injecting 200 million cubic feet per day (mmscfd) of gas back into the reservoir from which it has been produced, will be towed to the J-Block's Judy platform via Rotterdam on December 20.
It will be installed before the end of December, assuming a window of good weather from the time the barge carrying the module leaves Rotterdam.

"If we get a two or three day weather window we can do it", said Duncan Knight, senior project engineer in charge of marine installation. And first gas injection is anticipated on or before April 1, 1997.

Phillips, which holds 36.5 percent of the Judy/Joanne project in J-block with Agip (UK) Ltd (33 percent) and British Gas Exploration and Production (30.5 percent) says the module will give the company more flexibility in producing hydrocarbons from the field.
But Richard Vernon, director, external affairs at Phillips, agreed that the company would have preferred not to build the 40 million stg plant at all.
Enron is not happy with Phillips' solution to the problem.

In a written answer to a question seeking their reaction to the launching of the module, Enron said on Wednesday: "We do not know if Phillips plans to produce and reinject. We do not believe the J-Block parties are within their contractual rights to reinject and we have consistently notified them of this fact.
"The gas supply agreements require the J-Block parties to provide reservoir information and other information regarding reinjection.
"They have not provided all the information required, and based on the information received to date, they are not contractually entitled to reinject".

Enron and Phillips are currently involved in litigation over the date on which the payment obligations under the take-or-pay contract start. In May, the J-Block owners asked the U.K.'s High Court to declare that Enron could not refuse to agree a commissioning date, and so defer its obligations until the autumn of this year.

Enron said on Tuesday that "there are a number of issues currently at trial and we cannot comment on any of them individually". But the company added that the Appeal Court found in its favour in October with regard to the commissioning date litigation, although the J-Block parties have sought leave to appeal to the House of Lords.
At the root of the problem is the price of natural gas in Britain. Prices were higher when the contract was signed than they were when Phillips believes Enron's obligations started.

Phillips said in May that it wanted the High Court to get Enron to specify a commissioning date, so as to prevent Enron deferring its take-or-pay obligations "because of a fall in gas prices in the United Kingdom".
Enron and Phillips are currently cooperating over gas testing from J-Block.
From November 18, Phillips has been producing gas and supplying it to Enron at Teesside and this is expected to continue for around another week.
The two sides hope to produce gas from Judy at the rate of 300 mmscfd for at least three days to prove that they are each capable of handling these volumes.
